Til.	People with red hair who have put up with teasing or “fiery” stereotypes may be pleased to
learn that they appear to be winners from an evolutionary perspective. A large genetics study
has revealed that, in Europe, the gene for red hair has been actively selected for more than
10,000 years. The study did not aim to uncover the reasons for the trend, but focused on the
broader question of whether human evolution has plateaued since the advent of agriculture.
By analysing DNA from nearly 16,000 ancient human remains and more than 6,000 living
individuals, the scientists provided compelling evidence that, in fact, biological evolution has
continued apace.
The scientists identified 479 genetic variants that appear to have been favoured by natural
selection. Genes linked to red hair, fair skin, susceptibility to coeliac disease and variants that
lower the chance of diabetes, baldness and rheumatoid arthritis have all become more common
in our recent history. www.lawpreptutorial.com
“Perhaps having red hair was beneficial 4,000 years ago, or perhaps it came along for the ride
with a more important trait,” the researchers said. Previous research has shown that people
with red hair and fair skin can produce vitamin D more efficiently, for instance, which may
have conferred survival benefits in northern climates. Previously only about 21 instances had
been identified of genetic traits being multiplied by natural selection, including genes linked to
the ability to digest milk in adulthood. The dearth of evidence suggested directional selection
had been rare since modern humans arose in Africa about 300,000 years ago and began to split

into different population groups around the world. The latest study, which used an
unprecedented number of ancient DNA samples combined with sophisticated computational
techniques, revealed that evolutionary selection has driven the spread or decline of hundreds
of genes in West Eurasia, and that that selection has accelerated since people transitioned
from hunter-gatherer lifestyles to farming.
[Science; Word Count: 315]

VIII. India is learnt to be no longer inclined in hosting the COP33 climate meeting in 2028. India
had not formally bid for the event, but Prime Minister Narendra Modi had made the offer in
December 2023, during the COP28 meeting in Dubai. These meetings decide the global course
of action on climate change. COP, or Conference of Parties, is the annual meeting of the
signatories to the 1994 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). It also
serves as the meeting of the signatories to the 2015 Paris Agreement, and 1997 Kyoto
Protocol. Despite the fact that a COP33 cell had been set up under the Climate Change
division in the Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change last year to prepare the
country for hosting the event.

There was a growing realisation within the government that as the host and President of the
conference, India would be expected to champion and prioritise the global cause on climate
change which could sometimes come in conflict with its own national positions on many
climate-related issues. COP33 is due to carry out a Global Stocktake (GST) of climate actions
to assess how the world has progressed on the Paris Agreement target of keeping global rise in
temperatures within 1.5 or 2 degree Celsius from pre-industrial times. Countries are expected
to raise the ambition of their climate action based on this exercise. There is greater scrutiny on
the climate actions of the host country which is supposed to act as the global climate leader
during its presidency. Besides, global events in the last few years, on the climate front and
elsewhere, had substantially altered the climate negotiation landscape, with divisions between
countries on several issues getting sharpened. India itself has been taking strong positions on

had not formally bid for the event, but Prime Minister Narendra Modi had made the offer in
December 2023, during the COP28 meeting in Dubai. These meetings decide the global course

temperatures within 1.5 or 2 degree Celsius from pre-industrial times. Countries are expected
to raise the ambition of their climate action based on this exercise. There is greater scrutiny on
the climate actions of the host country which is supposed to act as the global climate leader
during its presidency. Besides, global events in the last few years, on the climate front and

SECTION III
X.	The Uniform Civil Code means one country one rule in matters of personal law. Civil Code
covers laws governing personal matters such as marriage, divorce, maintenance, adoption,
inheritance, succession and guardianship. Article 44 of the Constitution declares that the
State shall endeavour to secure for citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of
India. However, Article 44 is placed under the Directive Principles of State Policy and is not
enforceable by courts. The idea is to combine different personal laws into one common law
applicable to all citizens irrespective of religion, race, caste or community. At the same time, it
has been opposed on the ground that it may affect religious freedom under Articles 25 and 26.
India is a secular and diverse country where Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Parsis and other
communities are governed by separate personal laws. Hindus are governed by laws such as
the Hindu Marriage Act, Hindu Succession Act, Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act and
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, while Muslims are governed by the Shariat
Application Act, Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act and other personal law principles. This
lack of uniformity creates difficulties in matters of succession, divorce, inheritance, adoption
and maintenance, and makes it difficult for judges to apply one common standard of justice.
The Uniform Civil Code was debated in the Constituent Assembly. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, K.M.
Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar and others supported it as a step towards national unity,
secularism and social reform. However, due to strong opposition, especially from members
concerned about interference with Muslim personal law, it was placed only as a Directive
Principle. Supporters argued that religion should be separated from social relations and that
personal laws should not obstruct equality.
Uniform Civil Code is also closely linked with gender justice. Personal laws of different
communities have often placed women in an inferior position in matters of marriage, divorce,
maintenance and inheritance. Problems such as polygamy, desertion, cruelty and triple talaq
show how women may suffer under unequal personal laws. A common civil law can help
promote equality between men and women and reduce discrimination.
Goa is often cited as an example because it follows a uniform family law applicable to all
communities. The judiciary has also repeatedly discussed the need for UCC in cases such as
Shah Bano, Sarla Mudgal, Narasu Appa Mali and Lily Thomas. The Supreme Court has
supported the desirability of UCC, while also recognising that social acceptance and legislative
will are necessary for its implementation. [Constitutional Law-UNIFORM CIVIL CODE; Word
Count: 413]

X.	The Uniform Civil Code means one country one rule in matters of personal law. Civil Code
covers laws governing personal matters such as marriage, divorce, maintenance, adoption,
inheritance, succession and guardianship. Article 44 of the Constitution declares that the
State shall endeavour to secure for citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of
India. However, Article 44 is placed under the Directive Principles of State Policy and is not
enforceable by courts. The idea is to combine different personal laws into one common law
applicable to all citizens irrespective of religion, race, caste or community. At the same time, it
has been opposed on the ground that it may affect religious freedom under Articles 25 and 26.
India is a secular and diverse country where Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Parsis and other
communities are governed by separate personal laws. Hindus are governed by laws such as
the Hindu Marriage Act, Hindu Succession Act, Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act and
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, while Muslims are governed by the Shariat
Application Act, Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act and other personal law principles. This
lack of uniformity creates difficulties in matters of succession, divorce, inheritance, adoption
and maintenance, and makes it difficult for judges to apply one common standard of justice.
The Uniform Civil Code was debated in the Constituent Assembly. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, K.M.
Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar and others supported it as a step towards national unity,
secularism and social reform. However, due to strong opposition, especially from members
concerned about interference with Muslim personal law, it was placed only as a Directive
Principle. Supporters argued that religion should be separated from social relations and that
personal laws should not obstruct equality.
Uniform Civil Code is also closely linked with gender justice. Personal laws of different
communities have often placed women in an inferior position in matters of marriage, divorce,
maintenance and inheritance. Problems such as polygamy, desertion, cruelty and triple talaq
show how women may suffer under unequal personal laws. A common civil law can help
promote equality between men and women and reduce discrimination.
Goa is often cited as an example because it follows a uniform family law applicable to all
communities. The judiciary has also repeatedly discussed the need for UCC in cases such as
Shah Bano, Sarla Mudgal, Narasu Appa Mali and Lily Thomas. The Supreme Court has
supported the desirability of UCC, while also recognising that social acceptance and legislative
will are necessary for its implementation. [Constitutional Law-UNIFORM CIVIL CODE; Word
Count: 413]

questions.stimulus:
XI.	Homicide means killing of one human being by another human being. The word comes from
Latin terms “homo”, meaning man, and “cida”, meaning to kill. However, all homicide does not
amount to murder. Section 100 of the BNS deals with culpable homicide, which includes acts
causing death but not necessarily amounting to murder. Murder is also a form of homicide, but
it is graver, more intensive, and is punished more severely. Section 101 of BNS defines murder
and explains when culpable homicide becomes murder.
The main difference between culpable homicide and murder is based on intention, knowledge,
and the degree of certainty of death. If the person committing the act has complete knowledge
that the act will, in all probability, cause death, and still deliberately commits it with free will
and intention, the act amounts to murder. In culpable homicide not amounting to murder,
there may be intention to cause death or bodily injury, but there is no certainty that death will
necessarily follow. Section 100 of BNS uses the expression “likely to cause death,” while
Section 101 of BNS uses stronger expressions such as “sufficient in the ordinary course of
nature to cause death” and “so imminently dangerous that it must, in all probability, cause
death.” www.lawpreptutorial.com
The difference can be understood through examples. If Z hates X and merely prays for X’s
death, no offence is committed because prayer does not cause death. If Z pushes X into an
eight-foot pit and X dies, it may amount to culpable homicide if Z did not know that death was
certain. But if Z ensures that X receives no food, water, or air until death, it becomes murder
because death is the natural and certain consequence.
In Nara Singh Challan v. State of Orissa, the court held that Section 100 is the genus and
Section 101 is the species. In Reg v. Govinda, the accused struck his wife and placed his foot
on her chest, resulting in death, but the act was treated as culpable homicide not amounting to
murder because death was not necessarily likely in the ordinary course. In State of A.P. v. R.
Punnayya, the Supreme Court explained three degrees of culpable homicide: murder under
Section 300, culpable homicide under Section 304 Part I, and the least grave form under
Section 304 Part II.
Confusion arises because intention and knowledge are difficult to prove. Courts examine facts,
pre-planning, grave provocation, sudden fight, fear, or private defence. Cases such as Ram
Kumar v. State of Chhattisgarh, Bhagwan Singh v. State of Uttarakhand, and Macchi Singh
v. State of Rajasthan show how courts decide punishment based on the gravity, knowledge,
intention, brutality, and surrounding circumstances. [Criminal Law-Culpable Homicide and
Murder under BNS; Word Count: 443]

questions.stem:
A security guard, annoyed by repeated trespass, pushes an intruder from a low boundary wall
after a heated exchange. The intruder falls awkwardly, suffers a spinal injury, and later dies.
The guard says he only wanted to frighten him, not cause death. The prosecution argues that
because death resulted from the guard’s act, the case must at least be examined as culpable
homicide, even if facts may not support murder.
Which statement best captures the initial classification?

options.label: a
options.text: It cannot be homicide because the guard did not use a conventional deadly weapon.

options.label: b
options.text: It must be murder because death resulted from a deliberate physical act.

options.label: c
options.text: It is only civil negligence because anger cannot create criminal homicide liability.

options.label: d
options.text: It may be culpable homicide because Section 100 covers acts causing death.

questions.stem:
A factory owner locks an injured worker inside a sealed storeroom overnight to “teach him
discipline,” despite knowing the room has no ventilation, no water, and dangerous chemical
fumes. He refuses repeated requests from staff to open the door. By morning, the worker dies
from suffocation and toxic exposure. The owner argues that he never physically struck the
worker and only intended confinement. The prosecution argues that he knowingly created
conditions where death would, in all probability, result.
What is the strongest conclusion?

options.label: a
options.text:
It amounts to murder because he knowingly and deliberately caused conditions where
death was probable.

options.label: b
options.text:
It is only wrongful confinement because absence of direct physical assault prevents murder
liability.

options.label: c
options.text: It is only negligence because he did not expressly say that he wanted the worker dead.

options.label: d
options.text:
It is no offence because workplace discipline excuses confinement causing unintended
death.

questions.stem:
During a sudden roadside quarrel, Kunal stabs Arjun once in the thigh with a small knife to
stop him from chasing him. The wound unexpectedly cuts a major artery, and Arjun dies
before medical help arrives. Evidence shows Kunal did not aim at the chest, neck, or abdomen,
and witnesses confirm that he ran away immediately after one blow. The prosecution alleges
murder, while the defence argues there may be intention to cause injury but not certainty that
death would necessarily follow.
Which answer best fits?

options.label: a
options.text: It is murder because every intentional stab leading to death has certainty of death.

options.label: b
options.text:
It may be culpable homicide because injury was intended but death was not necessarily
certain.

options.label: c
options.text: It is no offence because only one blow was given during a sudden quarrel.

options.label: d
options.text: It is only civil wrong because death happened unexpectedly after a minor injury.

questions.stem:
In acriminal law exam, a student writes that culpable homicide and murder are two unrelated
offences with no conceptual overlap. Another student writes that murder is a graver form
within the broader category of culpable homicide, and every murder is culpable homicide
though not every culpable homicide is murder. The examiner asks which answer better
reflects the relationship between the two provisions as explained by courts.
Which response is most accurate?

options.label: a
options.text:
They are unrelated offences because murder and culpable homicide share no common legal
foundation.

options.label: b
options.text:
They are identical offences because every culpable homicide must receive the same
punishment as murder.

options.label: c
options.text: Section 299 is the genus and Section 300 is the species within that broader category.

options.label: d
options.text:
Section 300 is broader because every death-causing act automatically becomes murder
first.

questions.stem:
Dev ties his rival to a chair in an abandoned shed and leaves him there for thirty minutes
intending to frighten him, but returns and releases him safely. Later, in another incident, Dev
locks the same rival in an airtight metal container in summer heat, knowing there is no air
supply and rescue is impossible, causing death. In deciding whether the second act is murder
rather than lesser culpable homicide, what distinction should the court emphasise?

options.label: a
options.text:
Whether the victim was Dev’s rival, because personal rivalry alone decides murder
classification.

options.label: b
options.text:
Whether Dev later regretted the act, because remorse converts murder into lesser
homicide.

options.label: c
options.text:
Whether the act occurred indoors, because closed places automatically create murder
liability.

options.label: d
options.text: Whether intention, knowledge, and certainty of death show the graver offence of murder.

questions.stem:
During a wedding dispute, Imran suddenly sees his brother being beaten by three men. In
panic, he picks up an iron rod and strikes one attacker once on the head. The attacker dies.
Evidence shows no earlier enmity, no weapon brought from home, and no repeated blows, but
the prosecution argues that a head injury proves intention to murder. The defence claims the
act occurred in fear, sudden fight, and possible defence of another.
How should the court approach classification?

options.label: a
options.text:
Treat it as murder because death by head injury always proves intention beyond further
factual inquiry.

options.label: b
options.text:
Examine circumstances like sudden fight, fear, provocation, private defence, and absence
of pre-planning.

options.label: c
options.text:
Treat it as no offence because panic and fear automatically excuse every death-causing
assault.

options.label: d
options.text:
Ignore surrounding facts because intention and knowledge are presumed whenever a
person dies.

XII. The Indian Succession Act, 1925 primarily aims to consolidate the law applicable to intestate
and testamentary succession and to create clarity in situations where property devolves after
death. It mainly applies to Christians, Parsis, and persons governed by the Special Marriage
Act in certain cases. It generally does not apply to Hindus, Muslims, Buddhists, Sikhs, and
Jainas, except where specifically provided, as seen from provisions such as Sections 4, 29 and
58. Section 2 defines important terms such as will, executor, administrator, codicil and
probate. A will is the legal declaration of the intention of a testator regarding distribution of
property after death, while probate is a certified copy of a will granted by a competent court.
Domicile under Sections 4 to 19 plays a critical role in determining which law governs
succession, especially where property is located across different jurisdictions. Section 5
provides that succession to immovable property in India is governed by Indian law, while
succession to movable property is governed by the law of the domicile of the deceased. The Act
recognises domicile of origin, domicile of choice and declared domicile. It also states that a
person can have only one domicile, the domicile of origin continues until a new one is acquired,
a minor’s domicile follows that of the parent, and a married woman acquires the domicile of
her husband. Sections 20 to 22 further clarify that marriage does not automatically create
proprietary interest in the property of a spouse.
The Act also provides rules on consanguinity and kindred under Sections 23 to 28.
Consanguinity means relationship between persons descended from a common ancestor and
may be lineal or collateral. There is no distinction between paternal and maternal relations or
full blood and half blood, and posthumous children are included. Intestate succession under
Sections 29 to 49 applies where a person dies without a valid will. Property generally devolves
upon the spouse, lineal descendants and kindred. A widow gets one-third where lineal
descendants exist, one-half where only kindred exist, and the whole property where no
kindred exists. A husband has the same rights in the wife’s property.
For Parsis, Sections 50 to 56 create a separate scheme where property is divided among widow
or widower, children, parents and next-of-kin. Testamentary succession deals with wills.

Under Section 59, any major person of sound mind can make a will. A will made by fraud,

questions.stimulus:
XIII. Bailment is defined under Section 148 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 as the delivery of
goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that the goods shall, when
the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of
the person delivering them. The person delivering the goods is called the bailor, and the
person receiving them is called the bailee. The essence of bailment lies in transfer of
possession without transfer of ownership. Ownership remains with the bailor, while
possession is temporarily transferred to the bailee. Bailment relates only to movable property
and may arise even without a formal contract, as recognised in State of Gujarat v. Menon
Mohammad Haji Hasan.
For a valid bailment, there must be specific movable goods, delivery of goods, change of
possession, delivery for a specific purpose, and an obligation to return or dispose of the goods

as directed by the bailor. Delivery may be actual, symbolic or constructive. Mere custody does
not amount to possession, and therefore does not create bailment. In Indra Kumar v. State of
M.P., luggage placed on the roof of a bus did not create bailment due to lack of entrustment. In
Kaliaperumal Pillai v. Visalakshmi, no bailment was found where there was no effective
delivery. Bailment may be for the benefit of the bailor, bailee, or both, and may be gratuitous
or non-gratuitous.
The bailor is under a duty to disclose known faults in the goods under Section 150, bear
necessary expenses in gratuitous bailment under Section 158, and indemnify the bailee under
Sections 159 and 164. The bailee must take reasonable care under Sections 151 and 152, must
not make unauthorised use of the goods, must not mix the goods without consent, and must
return the goods after the purpose is fulfilled. Cases such as Houghland v. R.R. Low, Rampal
v. Gaurishankar, Shantilal v. Tara Chand, and Union of India v. Amar Singh explain the
standard of reasonable care.
The bailor has the right to terminate bailment, demand restoration of goods, and sue third
parties for damage. The bailee has rights to compensation, delivery according to directions,
and lien. Particular lien is recognised under Section 170, while general lien under Section 171
is available to bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys and policy brokers. A finder of goods is
treated as a bailee under Section 71 and may sell the goods under Section 169 in limited
circumstances. Bailment differs from sale because ownership is not transferred, and differs
from licence because bailment requires delivery and transfer of possession. [Indian Contracts
Act-Contract of Bailment; Word Count: 428]

questions.stimulus:
XIV. The 1956 Articles concerning the Law of the Sea were adopted by the International Law
Commission at its eighth session and submitted to the General Assembly as part of the
Commission’s report. The Commission considered that the law of the sea involved legal,
technical, biological, economic and political aspects, and recommended an international
conference to embody the results in conventions or other appropriate instruments. The draft
applies to the law of the sea in time of peace only, and the term “mile” means a nautical mile
of 1,852 metres. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The draft begins with the territorial sea. It states that the sovereignty of a State extends toa
belt of sea adjacent to its coast, called the territorial sea, and also extends to the air space over
it, its bed and subsoil. The Commission recognised that State practice on the breadth of
territorial sea was not uniform, but considered that international law did not permit extension
beyond twelve miles. The breadth was to be measured from the low-water line, subject to
special rules on straight baselines, bays, ports, roadsteads, islands, drying rocks, opposite
coasts, adjacent States and river mouths.

The Articles also recognise the right of innocent passage. Ships of all States may pass through
the territorial sea, but passage remains innocent only when the ship does not commit acts
prejudicial to the security of the coastal State or contrary to international law. Foreign ships
must comply with the coastal State’s transport and navigation laws. No charge may be levied
merely for passage, except for specific services rendered. The coastal State’s criminal and civil
jurisdiction over foreign ships during passage is limited, and warships may be required to give
prior authorisation or notification.
For the high seas, the draft defines them as all parts of the sea not included in the territorial
sea or internal waters. No State may validly subject any part of the high seas to its
sovereignty. Freedoms of the high seas include navigation, fishing, laying submarine cables
and pipelines, and overflight. Ships sail under the flag of one State only, and there must be a
genuine link between the ship and the flag State. The draft further deals with warship
immunity, safety of navigation, duty to render assistance, prevention of slave trade, repression
of piracy, right of visit, hot pursuit, conservation of living resources, submarine cables and
pipelines, contiguous zone control, and continental shelf rights for exploration and exploitation
of natural resources.
[International Law-United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS); Word
Count:405]

questions.stimulus:
XVI. The Supreme Court held that survivors of acid attacks, who were forced to consume acid and
suffered internal injuries without any visible scarring, will be considered acid attack victims
under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016. The bench of CJI Surya Kant
and Joymalya Bagchi said that the clarification would apply retrospectively from the day the
Act came into force and also informed the government that existing punishment for acid
attack had failed as a deterrent, suggested reversing the burden of proof onto the accused and
said acid sellers should be made co-accused in such cases. The order came in a petition filed by
Shaheen Malik, who herself was a survivor and had flagged a gap in law that was leaving out
an entire category of victims without access to state support.
The RPwD Act includes acid attack survivors in its list of specified disabilities. But the
definition it settled on was narrow. Under Schedule 2(zc) of the Act, an “acid attack victim” is
a person “disfigured due to violent assaults by throwing of acid or similar corrosive substance.”
Survivors who had acid forcefully ingested fell outside it. The court noted the problem was
that “the use of the term “disfigured” appears to confine the scope of external disfigurement of
the body, thereby excluding cases involving internal injuries or scarring caused by the
administration of acid.”
The injuries in such cases are equally severe. When acid is ingested, it burns the mouth,
throat, oesophagus, and stomach. The damage is quite often permanent. Malik’s petition
states that “the corrosive substance causes intense burns and significant harm to the internal
organs, particularly the gastrointestinal system. This often results in lifelong medical
complications, including the need for ongoing gastroenterological care. Victims of oral acid
ingestion may experience long-term issues such as difficulty eating, swallowing, and
digestion.”
The consequences of falling outside the purview of the RPwD Act are significant. A disability
certificate under the Act is the gateway to financial assistance, rehabilitation schemes,
medical support, etc. Without it, a survivor cannot access any of it. The petition called it a
“textbook example of under-classification, where a law purports to treat a class of persons but
arbitrarily excludes a sub-group that is identically situated for the purposes of the law.” The
only difference between the two groups, it argued, is the method of the attack—throwing vs
administering acid, rather than the nature and extent of harm. /Law; Word Count: 406]

XVII. When spring rolls around in the northern hemisphere, so do conversations about “No Mow
May.” Homeowners forgo mowing, allowing otherwise hidden flowers to bloom in your lawn,
increasing your yard’s biodiversity and providing food for pollinator concerns like these, No
Mow May ors like bees. However, scientists have increasingly questioned whether this trend,
which began in the United Kingdom, is compatible with United States lawns. Many U.S.
lawns are filled with non-native species like dandelions (Taraxacum officinale), which
Europeans colonists introduced to North America. These plants are not necessarily a good food
source for native pollinators as they lack certain important amino acids that make nectar and
pollen nutritious. Because of concerns like these, No Mow May has actually “become quite
controversial” in the U.S. I mean, who knew dandelions could be so controversial?
“No Mow May” started in 2018 as a campaign by the U.K. organization Plantlife. The group
originally coined the slogan to encourage local U.K. councils to manage green spaces more like
traditional hay meadows to increase biodiversity. Historically, workers who tended hay
meadows let them grow long throughout spring and most of the summer, only cutting them at
the end of summer to make hay. Plantlife picked May as the month to focus on for two main
reasons: May is the month that many U.K. grassland species start to flower (although climate
change is shifting that), and May is also when farmers traditionally removed animals from
hay meadows so they could grow. Plantlife suggested local authorities test out the hay meadow
management style with “No Mow May.”
Plantlife soon realized that the slogan was catching on with the public, and that “this could be
a really great way to engage the public about the importance of grasslands. In the U.K.,
“people’s lawns are often kind of relic grasslands,” and letting them grow can reveal native
flowers they didn’t know they had in their lawn. These flowers provide nectar and pollen for
native bees and other local pollinators that evolved alongside these plants. Plantlife chose May
for its campaign because it aligns with traditional hay meadow management, not because
there was specific scientific evidence about not mowing in May. Since the campaign started,
there has been at least one study examining its effects: In 2022, Ecological Solutions and
Evidence published a paper showing that un-mowed grassland plots in the U.K. produced
more nectar in mid-late May than mowed plots, providing more food for native pollinators. But
in the United States, the effects of No Mow May aren’t necessarily the same. /Environment;
